newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minesweeping, blockades could embroil Japan in war.
newsitem.headline: Minesweeping, blockades could embroil Japan in war.

text.p: Japan is fooling itself if it believes it can take on minesweeping and naval blockades outside its territory, as proposed in a recent report, and not be drawn into a shooting war, military analysts said on Monday.

Reviewing new proposals on Japan-U.S. military cooperation announced on the weekend, the analysts said the extensive measures amounted to a new Security Treaty that challenges the country's pacifist constitution.

Under the proposed guidelines, Japan may send warships to support U.S. military action against a third country in two types of operations: a naval blockade to enforce economic sanctions and minesweeping.

Although Japan's conservative government argues that such missions do not amount to offensive action, they open the way for Japan to be drawn into a war with North Korea or China that could result from a future quarrel with the United States.
Article 9 of the constitution bans Japan from using military force to settle any international dispute and Japan has said it can only use military force when attacked.
"As a matter of course, the country that laid the mines would attack minesweepers during a conflict," said a commentary in the daily Tokyo Shimbun on Monday.
"Whether Japan likes it or not, the Self-Defence Forces (Japan's military) will become embroiled in military action," the Tokyo Shimbun said.

The same could be said for naval vessels inspecting third-country ships trying to run a naval blockade. Boarding ships without consent can be construed as a belligerent act, as could using weapons to stop them in international waters.
Providing military intelligence, from Japanese Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) planes flying near a conflict zone, for example, could also be regarded as an act of war.
"The new guidelines provide an entirely new framework for defence cooperation in a regional conflict near Japan," wrote Masaru Honda, an analyst for the daily Asahi Shimbun.

"This is much more than a mere 'guideline.' The content amounts to a 'New U.S.-Japan Security Treaty' and means a sea change in Japan's defence policy which enables the Self-Defence Forces to take part in a foreign war," Honda wrote.

The proposals regarding minesweeping and naval blockade operations were included in an interim report on a review of the "Guideline for Defence Cooperation," a 1978 document being overhauled with a final version due by November.

The 1978 guideline only stipulated U.S.-Japan military cooperation in the event of a Soviet invasion of Japan and did not require Japan to play any military role in a regional conflict in the Far East, unless attacked.
Besides listing minesweeping and blockades, the interim report is intentionally vague regarding geography, the analysts said.

The document does not specify what it means by a "regional conflict in areas surrounding Japan." It does not say whether the new framework would be invoked in a conflict on the Korean Peninsula, the Taiwan Strait or the Spratly Islands.

Japanese government sources have said Japan took pains not to discuss the Taiwan Strait, meaning an armed conflict between China and Taiwan, or the Spratly Islands, which would also involve China, in the current review.
Tokyo fears that such discussions would alienate China. Beijing has also repeatedly warned that China should not be made a target of a re-defined U.S.-Japan military alliance.

"In any case, I hope this interim report to the guidelines will enliven discussion in the country and in parliament on defence laws and policies," top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said on Monday, stressing that the report was not final.
